sections.title: Why your voice sounds "wrong" on tape

items.q: Why do so many people hate hearing their recorded voice?
items.a: "How you sound to you is **not how you sound to others**." You hear yourself mainly through **bone conduction** (deeper, denser path); others hear you through **air conduction**. Recordings play back via air — so they sound alien even when nothing is "wrong."

items.q: How is this like hating photos of yourself?
items.a: You see the **mirror** daily (flipped habit view); photos show the view others see. Same pattern for voice: rare recording exposure feels "wrong" until you recalibrate — it's **physics and familiarity**, not a broken instrument.

items.q: How do you stop flinching every time you hear yourself?
items.a: Listen to your voice **regularly** (podcast episodes, recordings) so **perception and reception recalibrate** until internal and external sound converge. "It requires **time** for you to become more comfortable with that sound."

items.q: What happens if you keep skipping playback?
items.a: **Avoidance perpetuates discomfort** — skipping recordings keeps perception and reception **permanently misaligned**. When you hear a recording, **that is how you sound** to the world — same as video showing how you look.

items.q: Should you "fix" your voice before you accept it?
items.a: No — **mindset before technique**. Embrace your voice as a unique instrument tied to unique stories and value, then apply vocal habits. "You're a unique individual with a **unique instrument**… be you, do you."

items.q: Is hating your voice rare among podcasters?
items.a: Self-consciousness about your voice is **nearly universal** — especially painful for podcasters who must review their own audio. Discomfort is **normal and fixable**, not a sign your voice is broken.
